notes: MCP journeys. Each declares its own servers and the engine spawns them for real. Two fixtures, because they model different failures. Local journeys use e2e_tests/fixtures/stub-mcp-server.mjs, whose mode argument selects two tools, no tools, every call answering with a tool-level isError payload, or a process that exits non-zero before answering initialize -- the last two have no equivalent in the Rust fixture. Remote journeys use the checked-in mock-mcp-server binary over HTTP, which is the transport hosted servers use and the only one OAuth applies to, and which implements the OAuth handshake the stub does not. Both are already built by the lane. A remote server's port is assigned by the OS and read back before launch, so no journey names one. Registry-sourced servers are deliberately absent: KIRO_MCP_REGISTRY_URL_OVERRIDE is read only by the Rust engines, while this lane runs KAS and the TUI learns registry servers solely from KAS's status notification, so no scenario file can reach that path. Completing an OAuth handshake is out of reach from here: the authenticate action hands a regenerated URL to the clipboard for a browser, so a journey can cover the state and the action but not the transition to running.

scenarios.name: A configured MCP server is listed as running with its tool count
scenarios.description: One stub MCP server configured before launch -- asserts the panel names it, marks it running, attributes it to local config, and reports the number of tools it advertised
scenarios.observe: The tool count is the load-bearing assertion: reading the config is enough to name the server and call it local, but '2 tools' only appears once the client has spawned the process, completed the initialize handshake and read the tools/list reply. A server that is configured but never reached still lists, as the failed-server journey shows, so the name alone proves nothing about the connection. '0 tools' is asserted absent because that is what the same row shows when the handshake does not complete.

scenarios.name: A server that refuses to start is listed as failed, not hidden
scenarios.description: One MCP server whose process exits non-zero before answering initialize -- asserts the panel still lists it, marks it failed and reports no tools, rather than dropping it from the listing
scenarios.observe: A broken server must stay visible, because a user debugging one needs to see it and its state; silently omitting it is the failure this guards. What catches a server that starts anyway is the wait for 'failed', which expires -- the absent 'running' is a backstop for a row that reports both, and is safe to assert only because the one configured server here is the broken one. '0 tools' is asserted with a caveat rather than as proof: the Details cell shows a failure reason when one is reported and falls back to the tool count when none is, so this pins today's behaviour of reporting no reason at all. If a reason ever surfaces, this predicate is the one that should be replaced by it.

scenarios.name: An MCP server's tools join the tool list under its name
scenarios.description: Two servers, one advertising two tools and one advertising none -- asserts both tools appear namespaced to their server with their own descriptions, and that the server with no tools contributes no rows
verify: screen.contains:Echo a sentinel back for scenario assertions.
scenarios.observe: Both tool names carry the server that provided them, which is what keeps two servers exposing the same name distinguishable; one is waited on and the other asserted, so neither is a restatement of the other. The description comes from the server's own tools/list reply, so asserting it proves the listing is built from the handshake rather than from config. The absent '@emptyone/' only means something once that server is known to have connected, which is why the run waits for its '0 tools' row in the MCP panel first: without that wait the negative would hold just as well for a server still starting up. A provider that advertises nothing is otherwise caught by the wait for its tool.

scenarios.name: Calling an MCP tool gates for approval then returns a result to the model
scenarios.description: The model calls a tool provided by a stub MCP server -- asserts the approval gate appears, the argument reaches the tool card, the name resolves, and a tool result returns to the model
scenarios.observe: The argument is what the card keeps: 'value=MCP-SENTINEL-42' proves it survived the wire to the tool. The server's own reply text does NOT reach this frame -- an approved call collapses to a single line naming the tool and its argument, so asserting the result string here would fail on the success path; the error journey asserts a payload instead, because that path expands. Name resolution is proven by the wait for the approval gate: an unresolved name returns an error result without ever gating, so that step expires. 'McpCallDone.' is scripted on a turn that only fires once a tool result returns, and the absent 'is not available' is the backstop for a name that gates but still resolves to nothing.

scenarios.name: An MCP tool that fails surfaces the server's own message
scenarios.description: The model calls a tool on a server that answers every call with isError -- asserts the card expands and shows the text the server sent, rather than a generic failure
scenarios.observe: A failing MCP tool is the one path that puts the server's payload on screen: an approved call that succeeds collapses to its argument, while an error expands the card and renders what the server returned. That makes this the only place a journey can prove the reply text itself crossed the wire, and it is the case a user most needs readable -- a broken MCP tool is diagnosed from its own message. The sentinel embeds the argument, so it also proves the argument reached the server rather than the message being canned.

scenarios.name: A remote server demanding OAuth is reported as needing auth, with a way to do it
scenarios.description: A remote MCP server that requires OAuth on every request -- asserts the panel separates 'needs authentication' from both healthy and failed, and offers the authenticate affordance rather than leaving the user to guess
scenarios.observe: OAuth applies only to the remote transport, so this server is a real HTTP listener that rejects unauthenticated requests. The value is in the three-way distinction: both 'running' and 'failed' are asserted absent, because a server awaiting authorization is neither, and collapsing it into either is what leaves a user staring at a server that will never work or hunting a failure that is not one. 'Enter to authenticate' is asserted because a state the user cannot act on is only half the surface. Dropping the server's OAuth requirement flips the row to running, which fails the gate and the negative together.

scenarios.name: Choosing authenticate restarts the OAuth flow instead of failing or claiming success
scenarios.description: The authenticate action taken on a server awaiting OAuth -- asserts the request to restart the flow is accepted rather than reported as failed, and that the row keeps both its state and the action afterwards
scenarios.observe: Authorising a hosted MCP server finishes in a browser, so the handshake cannot complete from the terminal and this journey does not claim it does: the row is asserted to still read auth-required afterwards, and 'running' asserted absent. The load-bearing predicate is the absent failure: on this engine the clipboard confirmation is shown before the flow is restarted, so waiting on it proves only that the keypress was routed -- what proves the restart was accepted is that the error the rejection path would raise never appears, which is why the run waits out the reset before asserting. The URL itself is unassertable here: nothing renders it on the success path, and the fallback that would print it depends on whether the host has a clipboard tool. The kept Ctrl+y affordance is the difference between a user who can retry and one staring at a row that swallowed their keypress.
